title: Reference-Translation and the Weighted Dutta-Ray Algorithm for Claims Problems
affiliations: Universitat de Barcelona, Universitat Abat Oliva CEU and University of Barcelona

detail.title: Reference-Translation and the Weighted Dutta-Ray Algorithm for Claims Problems

declarations.funderStatement: The authors gratefully acknowledge financial support from the Spanish Ministerio de Ciencia, Innovación y Universidades through Grant PID2023-150472NB-I00/AEI/10.13039/501100011033, and from the Generalitat de Catalunya through Grant 2021-SGR-00306

detail.abstract:
The Dutta-Ray egalitarian solution for a convex transferable utility game (Dutta and Ray, 1989) selects the Lorenz-maximal allocation in the core and can be computed through a recursive average-worth algorithm. In this paper, we combine two elementary extensions of this procedure. The first extension translates a convex game by means of a modular game generated by a reference vector, applies the Dutta-Ray algorithm to the translated game, and then restores efficiency by adding back the reference vector. For the second extension, we adopt the weighted version of the Dutta-Ray algorithm for convex games introduced by Koster (1999, 2002). This weighted procedure is well defined for convex games and returns a core allocation. 
When applied to claims problems, these constructions provide a common cooperativegame-theoretic foundation for the broad family of egalitarian-in-deviation rules (Izquierdo and Rafels, 2026). In particular, the constrained equal awards rule (CEA), the constrained equal losses rule (CEL), the family of reverse Talmud rules, the weighted CEA and weighted CEL rules, and the proportional rule are all based on Dutta-Ray solutions and obtained by choosing suitable reference vectors and/or weights.

title: Clearing Conditional Commitments: Privacy, Specification, and Custody in a Clearinghouse for Interdependent Action
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Clearing Conditional Commitments: Privacy, Specification, and Custody in a Clearinghouse for Interdependent Action

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Generative AI was used to assist in drafting and typesetting this manuscript from the author's research notes and proposition drafts, in formalizing and cross-checking the proofs, and in adversarial verification of the results. The author developed the model, results, and arguments, reviewed the entire manuscript, and is responsible for all content, including every mathematical claim.

detail.abstract: Latent willingness of the form "I will, if enough of the right others will" has no standard clearing institution. We model a conditional-commitment clearinghouse: a platform that authenticates participants (accuracy q), verifies that their mutual conditions are jointly satisfiable (consensus integrity c), routes compatible counterparts to one another, and chooses three design dials-custody of principal γ, specification timing σ, and disclosure granularity k-before activating the coalition at a fixed point. Our central result is that the welfare-maximizing clearinghouse is minimal on all three dials at once: it holds no principal, fixes terms late, and discloses progress only through a k-anonymized aggregate. The result is stated with its boundary: it holds in a bounded high-authenticity, intermediate-integrity region, reverses on each axis outside it, and the three minimalisms are coupled in welfare magnitude rather than additively separable. Three further results discipline the disclosure claim. First, the privacy dial's screening cost is a genuine information-leakage object-the Shannon mutual information between coalition type and the k-anonymized support count-and full disclosure does not perfectly screen. Second, the masking advantage survives a refinement-free selection: under Carlsson-van Damme risk dominance no rationality parameter appears anywhere in the model, the revealed game's contested-regime collapse is exact, and masked momentum is sustained-proven at the deadline rung and for the smallest coalitions, conjecture-gated (and grid-verified) at interior rungs. Third, partial masking is constrained-optimal for a structural reason: a single disclosure dial necessarily bundles "this coalition is real" with "you are not pivotal," so-in a one-round theorem extended by a dynamic calibration-the interior optimum exists even where the unconstrained ideal would be full type-disclosure with zero pivotality leakage. We state three formal propositions with complete proofs, enumerate the open conjectures, and propose an administrable safe-harbor rule keyed to the mechanism's structure.

title: Beyond AI Detection: The Productive AI Integration Framework (PAIF) for Teaching, Assessment, and Student Engagement in Higher Education

detail.title: Beyond AI Detection: The Productive AI Integration Framework (PAIF) for Teaching, Assessment, and Student Engagement in Higher Education

detail.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (Generative AI) is rapidly transforming teaching, assessment, and student engagement in higher education. While existing discussions frequently focus on academic integrity, AI detection, institutional policies, and ethical concerns, comparatively less attention has been devoted to how AI can be integrated productively to support meaningful learning. This paper proposes the Productive AI Integration Framework (PAIF), a conceptual framework designed to guide the responsible integration of Generative AI within higher education. Adopting a Design Science perspective, the framework was developed in response to three interconnected educational challenges: cognitive dependency in AI-assisted learning, the assessment of authentic competence in environments where AI can generate sophisticated outputs, and passive student engagement with AI-generated content. PAIF integrates three complementary components. The Cognitive Offloading Framework distinguishes cognitive activities that should remain the responsibility of learners from those that may be productively supported by AI systems. The PAO Model (Process, Artifact, and Oral) provides a multidimensional approach for evaluating authentic competence beyond final outputs. The AI Engagement Spectrum conceptualizes student interaction with AI as a progression from passive answer consumption toward reflective inquiry and self-regulated learning. Drawing upon constructivism, cognitive offloading theory, authentic assessment, self-regulated learning, and metacognition, the framework offers a unified pedagogical perspective on productive AI integration. The paper contributes an integrated approach that shifts the focus from AI restriction and detection toward the design of learning environments that preserve reasoning, authentic competence, and meaningful engagement while leveraging the benefits of AI-assisted learning. The framework provides a foundation for future empirical research and practical implementation across diverse higher education contexts.

title: The Health System’s Collaboration with Other Sectors in Response to Cyclone Freddy in Blantyre and Phalombe Districts of Malawi: A Case Study of Cyclone Freddy 2023
affiliations: University of the Western Cape and University of the Western Cape

detail.title: The Health System’s Collaboration with Other Sectors in Response to Cyclone Freddy in Blantyre and Phalombe Districts of Malawi: A Case Study of Cyclone Freddy 2023
detail.abstract: Introduction: The occurrence of climate change-induced extreme weather events requires multisector collaboration for effective response. This study explores the health system collaboration with other sectors in Blantyre and Phalombe districts of Malawi during the Cyclone Freddy response. The aim was to gain an in-depth understanding of the strategies used, the coordination mechanisms, and the identified gaps to be addressed for effective future collaboration.Methods: Key informant interviews and focus group discussions were conducted with Directors and other senior officials from all sectors at district council level. The study was grounded in a framework for multisector and multilevel collaboration, drawing on data from key informant interviews and focus group discussions.Results: In total, eleven key informant interviews and four focus group discussions were conducted. The findings indicate partial collaboration across sectors, as some criteria were not fully considered or followed. These include the preconditions, key drivers, mechanisms, structures, administration, execution, and evaluation for effective multisector collaboration. In addition, the lack of interdependency, standard operating procedures, guidelines, and capacity building limited effective collaboration among sectors.Conclusion: There is partial collaboration among sectors at the district council level under decentralization. The study findings provide evidence that could support the establishment of viable multisector collaboration under decentralization in Malawi.

title: The One-Stop-Shop Is One Step in the Right Direction
affiliations: Fordham University School of Law

detail.title: The One-Stop-Shop Is One Step in the Right Direction
detail.abstract: In Brokering Safety, Sharma, Kadri, and Adler urge federal policymakers to impose on data brokers the greater duty of policing and stemming online stalking, harassment, and related abuse; that burden should not fall to victims, they argue. Their proposal would close the unevenness among state laws, shift the burden of oversight away from victims, and, importantly, ensure accountability at a systemic level, addressing gaps in enforcement that allow brokers to evade meaningful consequences. Yet, the one-stop-shop solution that Brokering Safety proposes also accedes to the core neoliberal presumption insofar as it individualizes harm. Online abuse, like dark patterns and surveillance pricing, is just one of the many inevitable consequences of the laissez-faire regulatory approach to commercial surveillance in the United States. Given the authors’ stated concern about information asymmetries, we might assume that they would turn to structural fixes like broad purpose limitations or data minimization rules that reduce the pecuniary incentive to traffic in personal data. Such measures have the added advantage of mostly avoiding the First Amendment hurdle to the extent they are neither content-based nor have incidental effects on the lawful distribution of truthful information. In the end, this short response essay argues that Sharma, Kadri, and Adler are right to attend to data broker harms, but their recommendations for reform are incomplete given the information asymmetries that motivate their intervention in the first place.

title: Adjudicating and Subjectivizing: The Role of Supranational Body in Governments’ Fiscal Transparency
affiliations: and Australian National University (ANU)

detail.title: Adjudicating and Subjectivizing: The Role of Supranational Body in Governments’ Fiscal Transparency
detail.abstract: Faced with fiscal constraints, many governments provide guarantees in public-private partnerships to incentivise private capital to complement public investment. While such guarantees enhance the creditworthiness of PPP projects, they also expose governments to significant fiscal risks if not properly accounted for and managed, raising concerns about fiscal transparency and accountability. This paper examines how accounting effects fiscal reform through its adjudicating and subjectivizing roles. Focusing on the International Monetary Fund’s efforts to promote fiscal transparency in Brazil, we analyse changes in government reporting of PPP guarantees and contingent liabilities following IMF monitoring. This study contributes to a better understanding of accounting’s roles in governance by demonstrating how supranational adjudication can drive national accounting change without coercive power, and how institutional logics shape a government’s subjectivizing behaviours. The findings have implications for international organisations seeking to foster fiscal transparency and for governments navigating external demands alongside domestic institutional logics.

title: Impact of Macroeconomic and Geopolitical Developments on the Implied Equity Risk Premium of Nifty 50
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Impact of Macroeconomic and Geopolitical Developments on the Implied Equity Risk Premium of Nifty 50
detail.abstract:
The Implied Equity Risk Premium (ERP) is a forward-looking measure of the additional return investors demand for investing in equities over risk-free securities. As it is derived from current market prices and expected future cash flows, it serves as an important indicator of investor sentiment and market risk perception. 

This study examines the impact of macroeconomic and geopolitical developments on the Implied ERP of the Nifty 50 Index during the period from 1 January 2026 to 15 June 2026. Using an aggregate valuation approach, the Nifty 50 is treated as a single economic entity, and the implied cost of equity is estimated through a discounted cash flow framework based on projected Free Cash Flow to Equity (FCFE). The Implied ERP is then determined by subtracting the risk-free rate from the estimated cost of equity. 

The analysis indicates that the Implied ERP remained relatively stable during the study period, averaging approximately 5.3%, while exhibiting fluctuations in response to significant economic, regulatory, and geopolitical events. Key developments such as the Union Budget 2026, regulatory announcements, and escalating tensions in the Middle East influenced investor expectations and market valuations. Sectoral analysis further highlights the significant role of Financial Services, Oil & Gas, and Information Technology sectors in shaping market risk perceptions. 

The findings demonstrate that the Implied ERP is an effective real-time measure of investor sentiment and provides valuable insights into the relationship between market valuation, risk perception, and external economic developments in the Indian equity market

title: The Geometry of Flat Payoffs in First-price Auctions

detail.title: The Geometry of Flat Payoffs in First-price Auctions

keywords: Flat Payoff Property JEL Classification: C72

detail.abstract: Why do bidders in first-price auctions systematically deviate from Nash equilibrium bids, yet suffer negligible losses? This paper addresses this puzzle by providing a structural characterization of the Flat Payoff Property in symmetric environments. I define a Payoff Flatness Index, the reciprocal of the local curvature of the interim utility function, that fully characterizes a bidder's strategic insensitivity to bid deviations. I prove that while payoff landscapes eventually flatten for all interior types, this transition is non-monotonic. For high-valuation bidders, additional competition initially steepens the payoff landscape before the declining probability of winning asymptotically dominates. A closed-form decomposition of the curvature isolates three channels driving this result: probability decay, degrees of freedom, and shading compression. The findings establish that strategic insensitivity is a structural consequence of the first-price mechanism itself, not a behavioral anomaly requiring non-standard preference. The results reconcile decades of experimental findings with standard equilibrium theory.

detail.abstract:
Background: Breast and thyroid nodules are among the most common lesions encountered in ultrasound practice and account for a substantial diagnostic workload worldwide. Current artificial intelligence (AI) systems are largely restricted to single-organ assessment using static images and have shown limited integration into routine clinical workflows. We developed and validated NoduleNet, a unified AI framework for real-time detection, binary risk classification, and guideline-based risk stratification of breast and thyroid nodules from ultrasound video streams.

Methods: In this multi-center diagnostic study, 15,332 ultrasound videos (9,596 breast and 5,736 thyroid examinations) from four hospitals were retrospectively collected for model development and external validation. NoduleNet incorporated spatiotemporal feature extraction and cross-organ transfer learning to enable unified analysis of breast and thyroid nodules. Model performance was evaluated for lesion detection, binary risk classification, and guideline-based risk stratification according to ACR BI-RADS and C TI-RADS. Clinical utility was prospectively assessed in a fully crossed multi-reader, multi-case study involving 281 ultrasound videos and nine radiologists with varying levels of experience.

Findings: On the independent test set, NoduleNet achieved F1 scores of 0·851 for breast nodule detection and 0·880 for thyroid nodule detection. For binary risk classification, the model achieved an AUC of 0·895 (95% CI: 0·855-0·934) for breast nodules and 0·816 (95% CI: 0·784-0·849) for thyroid nodules. Corresponding AUCs for BI-RADS and TI-RADS risk stratification were 0·782 (95% CI: 0·716-0·841) and 0·704 (95% CI: 0·655-0·751), respectively. In the prospective reader study, AI assistance significantly improved lesion detection, diagnostic consistency, and workflow efficiency across all experience levels, with the greatest benefits observed among junior radiologists. AI-assisted junior radiologists achieved diagnostic performance approaching that of unassisted senior radiologists while reducing interpretation time by more than 40%.

Interpretation: NoduleNet enables accurate real-time ultrasound interpretation of breast and thyroid nodules within a single unified framework. By combining dual-organ analysis, video-based assessment, and prospective clinical validation, the system improves diagnostic performance, reduces inter-observer variability, and enhances workflow efficiency. These findings support the integration of AI-assisted ultrasound interpretation into routine nodule screening and risk assessment pathways.

title: Do AIs Make Good Traders, and Do They Make Good Traders Better?
affiliations: , Elm Partners and Elm Partners

detail.title: Do AIs Make Good Traders, and Do They Make Good Traders Better?
detail.abstract:
Recent advances in large language models have renewed interest in the idea that artificial intelligence can predict market movements from news and other public information. This article examines that premise through a practical lens, exploring whether modern AI systems can consistently generate trading profits in highly competitive financial markets. Drawing on evidence from market efficiency, behavioral finance, and empirical testing, the discussion highlights the distinction between information processing and investment success. While AI excels at rapidly synthesizing vast amounts of data, markets quickly incorporate widely available information, limiting the persistence of purely predictive advantages.

The article argues that the greatest value of AI in investing may lie not in forecasting returns, but in improving decision-making processes, enforcing discipline, reducing behavioral biases, and enhancing portfolio construction and risk management. It further emphasizes the challenges posed by transaction costs, crowding effects, model overfitting, and the adaptive nature of financial markets, all of which can erode apparent predictive edges. The conclusion suggests that AI is likely to become an increasingly important tool for investors, but one that complements rather than replaces sound investment principles. Long-term investment outcomes may depend less on finding a perfect forecasting model and more on using AI to support robust, systematic, and evidence-based decision-making.

title: Preeclampsia Prevention by Risk-Stratified Timed Birth: A Bayesian Analysis

detail.abstract:
Background: PREVENT-PE was a trial (n=8,094 women) comparing usual care with planned timed birth between 37 and 40 weeks’ gestation, based on risk stratification for preeclampsia (PE) at 35–36 weeks. In the intervention group, there was a 30% reduction in birth with PE, without an increase in emergency cesarean or neonatal unit (NNU) admission for ≥48 hours. 

Methods: This post hoc Bayesian analysis evaluates the impact of the intervention within each PE risk stratum in 4,734 participants from one study site where biobanked samples and hemodynamic assessments were available, permitting calculation of PE risk. Outcomes were birth with PE (primary trial outcome), and emergency cesarean and NNU for ≥48 hours (key secondary outcomes). 

Findings: Birth with PE incidence was 5.7% (95% credible interval [CrI], 4.7-6.8) in the control group and 4.1% [3.4-4.9] in the intervention group, for a posterior median incidence ratio of 0.72 [0.56-0.93] and a posterior probability-of-benefit of 0.995, consistent in direction and magnitude with those of the primary PREVENT-PE trial. However, overall benefit was driven primarily by the 39- and 40-week strata (posterior probabilities-of-benefit 0.985 and 0.992, respectively), with little evidence of excess NNU admission for ≥48 hours (posterior probability-of-harm 0.651 and 0.679, respectively), but a potential increase in emergency cesarean in the 39-week but not 40-week groups (posterior probability-of-harm 0.857 and 0.353). There was little evidence of benefit in 37- and 38-week strata (posterior probabilities-of-benefit, 0.463 and 0.622, respectively), and some evidence of excess NNU admission for ≥48 hours (posterior probabilities-of-harm, 0.746 and 0.825, respectively), but substantial uncertainty due to small numbers. 

Interpretation: Risk stratification with timed birth was associated with evidence of benefit in 39- and 40-week strata, with little suggestion of neonatal harm. In 37- and 38-week strata, there was no evidence of benefit, but potential neonatal harm consistent with early-term birth.

detail.abstract:
Background: Pressure injury (PI) staging is subjective, variable between raters, and harder in darker skin, even though PIs fall disproportionately on darker-skinned patients. Deep learning staging models exist but are built largely on small, curated public datasets, seldom tested on real-world images, and never evaluated across diverse skin tones.

Methods: We first audited labels in two public datasets (PIID and Roboflow) using confident learning with physician adjudication. In this retrospective, observational study, we then assembled a real-world cohort of 33 342 wound photographs from 3178 inpatients at a US health system and derived per-image NPIAP stage labels from clinical notes using a weakly supervised vision-language pipeline. We trained four-class and six-class staging models, evaluated cross-domain generalisation, and estimated skin tone from perilesional skin (validated against human raters) to assess subgroup performance on physician-labelled test sets.

Findings: Confident learning flagged 267 of 3104 public images (8·6%); 75·3% were actionable on physician review, and cleaning improved macro-F1 by 3·1–4·9 points across all eight architectures. A public-trained model scored 88–89% macro-F1 in-domain but 47·8% on bedside photographs. Note-derived labels agreed moderately with physicians (43·0%; 93·7% within one stage), yet models trained on them alone reached 75·3% macro-F1, exceeding physician-only training by 21·0 points; the combined four-class model reached 76·7% (AUROC 93·7%) and the six-class cascade 66·8%. Tone estimation was reliable for 98·8% of inpatient but ≤84% of public images, and biased darker on the latter. On validated test sets, we did not detect statistically significant performance differences across skin-tone groups, though per-tone subgroups were small.

Interpretation: Models that perform well on curated public benchmarks perform substantially worse on bedside images, and their labels and skin-tone composition are too unreliable for development or fairness evaluation. Deriving labels from routine documentation yields real-world, skin-tone-diverse training data and enabled the first evaluation of pressure injury staging across skin tone, establishing foundations for prospective clinical testing.

title: Why Technological Monopoly Rent does not Decay

detail.title: Why Technological Monopoly Rent does not Decay

detail.abstract: A standard expectation in economics is that monopoly returns are self-limiting. Entry, imitation, competition, and diffusion are supposed to compete excess returns away, so that any gap between price and the cost of provision is a transient disequilibrium rather than a durable structure. This paper argues that the classical decay expectation fails for the central productive assets of the artificial-intelligence economy: frontier compute, trained model weights, and the data-and-feedback advantages that accrue to incumbents. It fails on the classical theory's own terms rather than by special pleading. I first reconstruct the decay mechanism as a three-layer theorem (Marshall's reproducible quasi-rent, the contestable-markets discipline, and Schumpeterian creative destruction), then show that each layer rests on a premise that does not hold for AI-era assets. The shared root of the three failures is that the corrective force every classical mechanism relies on is external to the rent, whereas here the rent has internalized its own correctives. The surplus finances the rising reproduction threshold, the sunk-cost structure forecloses the hit-and-run entrant, and the incumbent owns the inputs of the next innovation wave, with demand-side platform lock-in compounding all three. Scale economies, capital-intensity at the frontier, increasing returns to data, and a "speed problem" in which the technology re-arrives faster than institutions can respond reinforce the result: a rent with no internal mechanism of decay. So concentration in this domain does not self-correct, and the gap between what is technically abundant (cognitive output at marginal cost approaching zero) and what is priced as scarce (metered access) widens rather than closes as the productive forces advance. I am careful to mark the limit of the claim. The absence of an internal solvent is a structural result; whether an external solvent (an efficiency shock, a demand saturation that never arrives) reopens competition is a forecast, not a theorem. The argument develops the second of two original results in An Invitation After Abundance (Chen 2026, ISBN 979-8-9960105-0-9); the first, the derivation of the rent category itself, is developed separately and is not the subject of this paper.

detail.title: Beyond reimbursement: nurse practitioner remote monitoring adoption in National Medicare data
detail.abstract: BackgroundRemote physiologic monitoring and remote therapeutic monitoring are reimbursable Medicare services that could extend chronic care and rehabilitative monitoring beyond clinic walls. Nurse practitioners are a major primary care and specialty workforce, but their use of these billing pathways has not been described nationally.ObjectiveTo quantify nurse practitioner billing for remote monitoring in Medicare and examine variation by state practice environment and rural-urban geography. Design: Cross-sectional secondary analysis of 2024 public-use Medicare provider-service data.SettingsUnited States Medicare fee-for-service billing records.Participants976,337 nurse-practitioner provider-service records; the primary policy analysis was restricted to the 50 states and District of Columbia and included 187,611 nurse practitioner provider-sites.MethodsRemote monitoring was identified with Healthcare Common Procedure Coding System codes for remote physiologic monitoring and remote therapeutic monitoring. Outcomes were provider-site adoption, services per 100,000 nurse practitioner services, nonunique beneficiaries, and estimated Medicare payment. State practice environment and rural-urban commuting area groups were examined descriptively, with prespecified sensitivity analyses.ResultsIn 2024, 994 nurse practitioner provider-sites billed remote monitoring, 0.53% (0.50-0.56), accounting for 411,179 services, 103,908 nonunique beneficiary counts, and $12,019,403 in estimated Medicare payment. The overall service rate was 251.6 per 100,000 nurse practitioner services. Remote physiologic monitoring accounted for 402,009 services, whereas remote therapeutic monitoring accounted for 9,170 services (2.2% of remote monitoring services). Full-practice states had 372.0 remote monitoring services per 100,000 nurse practitioner services and 0.70% (0.63-0.77) provider-site adoption; reduced-practice states had 178.6 and 0.40% (0.35-0.45); restricted-practice states had 222.0 and 0.50% (0.45-0.56). The top 1% of remote-monitoring provider-sites accounted for 11.2% of services.ConclusionsNP remote monitoring adoption in Medicare was measurable but uncommon in 2024, dominated by remote physiologic monitoring, and uneven across policy and geographic contexts. Practice authority may enable adoption but is unlikely to be sufficient without organizational, billing, technology, and patient-access infrastructure.

title: The fair-weather hedge: why a sovereign oil importer’s natural price cushion fails in the tail, and what that means for hedging

detail.title: The fair-weather hedge: why a sovereign oil importer’s natural price cushion fails in the tail, and what that means for hedging
detail.abstract: A large oil importer cannot trade away its core energy exposure: the monthly crude-import bill is a non-tradable physical requirement fixed by national demand, not a portfolio to be re-weighted. We argue that this object carries a feature the risk literature has largely overlooked, and which inverts conventional hedging advice. Because a major importer sources part of its crude at a discount to the prevailing benchmark, its realised bill embeds a natural hedge that suppresses variance in calm months but is state-dependent: it compresses or vanishes precisely in the crises against which protection is most wanted. Using India as the application, we measure the bill’s tail risk with a regime-aware filtered-historical-simulation model and quantify this embedded hedge directly. On the October-2025 import book the 99 percent monthly expected shortfall is US$15.8 billion, exceeding a full month’s bill; the realised sourcing discount is worth on the order of US$2 billion in a stressed month but is negatively correlated with the worst tail. The central implication is that a sovereign must size its financial hedge to the residual exposure after the natural hedge is assumed absent, not to the calm-state bill: the cushion that justifies a smaller hedge is exactly what fails when the hedge is needed. The framework is reproducible from public data and portable to other import-dependent economies.   Keywords: value-at-risk; expected shortfall; filtered historical simulation; crude oil; import bill; energy risk; backtesting JEL: C58, G32, Q41, Q43

title: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Optimizing Care Pathways in Patients with Complex Chronic Conditions
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Optimizing Care Pathways in Patients with Complex Chronic Conditions
detail.abstract: Complex chronic conditions (CCCs), comprising one of the main causes of morbidity and mortality, are often managed through predefined care pathways. These pathways advocate the application of therapeutic guidelines according to disease progression in order to enhance patient outcomes while minimizing costs. Considering patient heterogeneity, however, demands the establishment of tailored pathways. This work proposes a multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) framework able to derive such pathways for representative patient groups characterized by a set of comorbidities, along with their clinical roles, who interact toward common objectives.

title: The Collapse of Digital Consent: A Legal Examination of India's Viral Privacy Crisis
affiliations: and National Law University, Jodhpur

detail.title: The Collapse of Digital Consent: A Legal Examination of India's Viral Privacy Crisis
detail.abstract:
Abstract

The rise of non-consensual dissemination of intimate images (NCII) in India highlights the serious inadequacies of the law and education in the digital era. India has no specific law to address NCII, despite its proven impact on women, with over 19,510 cases reported in 2023 and tragic incidents like leaker-related suicide cases and AI-generated abuse repeatedly reported. Current provisions in the Indian Penal Code (IPC), Sections 354C and in the Information Technology (IT) Act, Sections 66E and 67, are fragmented, with consensual pornography and image-based abuse not being clearly differentiated, nor is consent the primary legal factor.

The article reviews the legal vacuum that facilitates digital voyeurism and suggests that the normalisation of deviance, in which harmful behaviour becomes culturally accepted without being punished, contributes to the crisis. The article draws on feminist legal theory and comparative analysis of the United Kingdom, the United States, Australia and Ireland to show that action on all three fronts is necessary to make effective responses: specific criminalisation of NCII and disclosure threats, accessible fast-track takedown mechanisms and mandatory consent education in schools.

From a constitutional perspective, violations of NCII rights raise issues of the rights to privacy, dignity, and autonomy, and conflict with free expression under Article 19. The article calls for a doctrinal development in which digital privacy harms can be considered fundamental constitutional issues, and suggests specific reforms such as statutory clarity, platform accountability under the IT Rules 2021, and preventive digital literacy programmes. In any legal action, there needs to be a balance between the protection of victims and the dangers of over-censorship and surveillance abuse; otherwise, the dignity of expression in the digital world will be lost.

title: Why Low-Rank Causal Discovery Works: Identifiability, Minimax Rates, and the Capacity Bottleneck

detail.title: Why Low-Rank Causal Discovery Works: Identifiability, Minimax Rates, and the Capacity Bottleneck

detail.abstract: Low-rank factorization of the adjacency matrix (W = U V ⊤ with U, V ∈ R d×r , r ≪ d) reduces the computational complexity of causal discovery from O(d 3) to O(dr 2). While empirical benchmarks show that LowRankGNN recovers true edges at d up to 10 8-far beyond the d ≈ 150 collapse point of classical NOTEARS-the theoretical understanding of when and why low-rank causal discovery works has been absent. We provide five contributions: (i) Under a low-rank true adjacency matrix, we prove that the NOTEARS objective with low-rank parameterization identifies the true causal order up to linear equivalence (Theorem 1). (ii) We establish a sample complexity of n = Ω(dr log d/ϵ 2), compared to n = Ω(d 2 log d/ϵ 2) for dense methodsa reduction by a factor of d/r (Theorem 2). (iii) We prove that this rate is minimax-optimal by constructing a lower bound via Fano's inequality over the low-rank DAG class (Theorem 3). (iv) We show that the rank-r factorization serves as the tightest convex relaxation of the DAG constraint on the low-rank manifold, explaining why LowRankGNN converges reliably where dense NOTEARS diverges (Theorem 4). (v) We validate all theoretical predictions on synthetic benchmarks (d = 50-1000, r = 2-32) and the TCGA pan-cancer collection (d = 150, 33 cancer types). Together, these results establish the low-rank parameterization as a provably optimal representation for differentiable causal discovery.

detail.abstract:
Background: Persistence of Ebola virus (EBOV) in survivors has been linked to new outbreaks and the prolongation of existing Ebola virus disease (EVD) outbreaks months to years after they are declared over, highlighting the need for preventive strategies beyond reactive response. Vaccination of survivor networks has been proposed as a preventive strategy,however limited evidence exists on the operational feasibility of this approach. The objective was to evaluate a preventive EVD vaccination strategy targeting survivor networks and assess its operational feasibility and programmatic implications.

Methods: In 2024, a targeted preventive EVD vaccination campaign was implemented in the Equateur Province, Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), focusing on individuals identified through survivor networks. Networks were mapped using confidential, survivor-led elicitation processes adapted from contact tracing and HIV partner-notification approaches. Microplanning was conducted to estimate target populations, followed by field-based listing to confirm target populations. Eligible individuals were offered a single dose of rVSVΔG-ZEBOV-GP vaccine. Vaccination data were recorded using paper registers and DHIS2.

Findings: Of 94 registered survivors, 89 were successfully mapped. Survivor-network mapping and listing identified 17,577 individuals, of whom 14,445 were unvaccinated and eligible. A total of 10,084 individuals were vaccinated across 45 fixed sites or health posts, corresponding to 69.8% coverage among eligible individuals. The eligible population exceeded initial planning estimates, reflecting the broad scope of survivor-network identification. Vaccine wastage was minimal (0 6%), and no serious adverse events were reported.

Interpretation: Preventive EVD vaccination targeting survivor networks was operationally feasible in a post-outbreak setting and achieved substantial uptake among eligible individuals. This approach may offer a preventive strategy to mitigate the risk of EVD re-emergence associated with persistent EBOV infection in survivors. These findings support consideration of survivor-network vaccination within national EVD preparedness strategies in outbreak-prone settings.

title: The Other Side of the Calculation Argument: Information Minimality as a Design Principle

detail.title: The Other Side of the Calculation Argument: Information Minimality as a Design Principle

detail.abstract: Mises (1920, 1949) established the necessity of market prices for rational economic calculation. Reconstructed in information-theoretic language, the argument is a floor claim, below which rational economic calculation is impossible. The argument has an unrecognised dual. Mechanisms that operate on more information than coordination requires are not merely inefficient. They reproduce, from the opposite direction, the same pathologies Mises identified in socialist planning. These are centralisation pressure, surveillance exposure, epistemic fragility, and behavioural distortion. The correct design target, on Austrian premises, is the minimum sufficient information set, enough to permit coordination. Hayek (1945) pointed in this direction, observing that the price system communicates only what coordination requires. The present paper states the architectural dual. A constructive existence proof in Armstrong (2026a) identifies declared category and aggregate outcome as a sufficient signal architecture for a class of designed coordination mechanisms, arguing that no categorical mechanism meeting the same welfare and detection targets can use less category entropy. Less breaks coordination. More degrades it. Privacy, for the operation of the mechanism, is a corollary. What lies outside the minimum sufficient set was never part of what coordination required. The boundary is structural, not imposed.

title: The Road Less Traveled: Effects of Congestion Pricing on Collisions and Injuries in New York City

detail.title: The Road Less Traveled: Effects of Congestion Pricing on Collisions and Injuries in New York City
detail.abstract: This paper estimates the effects of New York City's congestion pricing policy on motor vehicle collisions and traffic-related injuries. Using geo-located crash data, the analysis finds that during weekday peak hours within the Congestion Relief Zone (CRZ), crashes per ZIP-hour-day declined by approximately 69 percent, corresponding to roughly 12 fewer crashes and 8 fewer injuries per weekday peak period. Back-of-the-envelope calculations suggest daily peak-hour medical cost savings of approximately $52,000, with larger gains when broader social costs are considered. Heterogeneity within peak hours shows that pedestrian injuries increased during the morning commute but declined in the evening, consistent with changes in pedestrian density and a relatively inelastic demand for arriving at work on time. Off-peak estimates indicate an isolated increase in crashes and injuries within the CRZ. Weekday net effects show congestion pricing improving roadway safety inside the CRZ while increasing crash and injury risk above the boundary, suggesting possible crash displacement to nearby, untolled areas.

title: Random Utility Model with Endogenously Assigned Menus

detail.title: Random Utility Model with Endogenously Assigned Menus
detail.abstract: There is a largely overlooked assumption underlying stochastic choice theory: menus are assigned exogenously, as if by a hidden randomized controlled trial. This assumption is not innocuous, because in many real-world settings menus are assigned endogenously according to the decision makers' preferences. This paper studies Random Utility Model under menu endogeneity and shows that any seemingly anomalous choice behavior can be generated by a population of rational decision makers with heterogeneous preferences facing endogenously assigned menus. To address this problem, I propose a new causal estimand: the probability that an alternative would be chosen from a given menu if that menu were presented to the entire population. I then characterize sharp bounds on this estimand using observed menu and choice frequencies. In addition, I show that when choices are observed across multiple markets with different preference distributions and a common menu-assignment rule, the causal estimands from those markets and the menu assignment rule are uniquely identified.

title: Evidence-Based Allocation of Emergency COVID-19 Support: A Real-World Policy Case from the Scottish Snowsports Sector
affiliations: University of Glasgow and

detail.title: Evidence-Based Allocation of Emergency COVID-19 Support: A Real-World Policy Case from the Scottish Snowsports Sector
detail.abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic confronted governments with the challenge of allocating scarce emergency public resources rapidly while balancing immediate financial need, organisational viability and longerterm regional resilience. Although considerable attention has been devoted to the economic consequences of the pandemic and the principles of evidence-based policymaking, less research has examined how such principles can be translated into operational decision frameworks capable of supporting funding allocation under conditions of severe uncertainty. Between 2020 and 2021, the first author undertook an independent programme of economic analysis on behalf of Snowsport Scotland that informed discussions with the Scottish Government and participating enterprise agencies during the development of the Scottish Ski Centre Fund. This paper documents the evidence-based analytical framework developed to support that process. Operational performance is benchmarked against comparable Nordic ski resorts using stochastic frontier analysis and integrated with financial assessment, business viability and strategic importance within a structured evidence-synthesis framework designed to support transparent and consistent funding recommendations. Rather than proposing a mechanical allocation rule, the framework combines quantitative analysis with structured expert judgement to distinguish temporary financial distress from longer-term structural considerations and to recognise the wider role of strategically important rural infrastructure. The paper therefore provides a rare contemporaneous account of academic economic research informing public policy during an unfolding crisis. More broadly, it offers a transferable framework for allocating emergency public resources that is applicable to other sectors where preserving rural resilience and productive capacity forms an important public policy objective.

title: Do Carbon Emissions and Transparency Affect Firms' Access to Finance?
affiliations: University of Glasgow and University of Glasgow

detail.title: Do Carbon Emissions and Transparency Affect Firms' Access to Finance?
detail.abstract: Climate change is increasingly becoming a financial concern as lenders reassess the risks associated with carbon-intensive business models. Firms with higher emissions may face tighter financing conditions due to expected transition costs arising from carbon pricing, environmental regulation, technological change, and shifting consumer preferences. At the same time, reducing emissions often requires substantial investment, creating particular challenges for financially constrained firms. This study examines whether carbon emissions affect firms' access to external finance and whether transparency mitigates any adverse financing effects. Using a sample of U.S. publicly listed non-financial firms from 2010 to 2023, the analysis measures emission intensity as carbon emissions scaled by total assets and captures access to finance through leverage, long-term debt, and the cost of debt. Transparency is proxied by segment-level disclosure, which provides lenders with more detailed information about firms' operating activities and environmental exposure. The study also considers loan-supply conditions to assess whether the role of transparency varies when credit becomes more scarce. The results indicate that firms with higher emission intensity generally exhibit lower debt capacity and higher borrowing costs. However, greater transparency weakens these adverse effects, particularly during periods of tighter loan supply. The findings highlight the importance of both environmental performance and information quality in determining firms' access to external finance during the transition to a low-carbon economy.

title: Food Rescue Greece: An Innovative Application for Tackling Food Waste
affiliations: University of West Attica

detail.title: Food Rescue Greece: An Innovative Application for Tackling Food Waste
detail.abstract: Every day, large quantities of edible food are discarded by catering establishments, hotels, food stores, and other businesses. On an environmental scale, this phenomenon generates waste and greenhouse gas emissions. However, digital technology can serve as a powerful tool in this fight. Today's mobile applications and websites are designed to help both local and global social and economic entities communicate and cooperate, enabling efficient resource management and information exchange. This paper presents the Food Rescue Greece application, a digital platform that allows businesses to donate surplus food to organizations and individuals in need of nutritional support. The application facilitates the collection, management, and redistribution of food that would otherwise be discarded. The main objective of this paper is to introduce a theoretical framework regarding food waste and to analyze the proposed application as an innovative solution for achieving social, economic, and environmental benefits.

title: Identifying Central Individuals without Social Network Information
affiliations: , University of Zurich - Faculty of Economics, Business Administration and Information Technology, University of Zurich, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Université Félix-Houphouët-Boigny, ETH Zürich, University of Zurich, Université Félix Houphouët-Boigny, University of Zurich and University of Zurich - Department of Business Administration

detail.title: Identifying Central Individuals without Social Network Information
detail.abstract: By targeting central individuals in a social network, marketers and policymakers can design seeding interventions that promote information diffusion, product adoption, or behavior change. Social network analysis allows the identification of central individuals, however complete social network information is often unavailable or costly to collect. Two strategies are commonly used in the absence of complete network information: one-hop sampling and social sensing. Yet, these two strategies have not been compared on the same networks, and previous work offers conflicting predictions on which identifies more central individuals (higher-degree seeds). We provide a direct comparison of the two strategies, using original data from a cocoa-farming village in Côte d'Ivoire (502 adults) and public data from 33 villages in India (6,464 households) and 11 classrooms in Spain (487 students). We report two findings. First, social sensing identifies seeds with 9 to 58 percent higher degree than one-hop sampling across all three settings. Second, conditional on degree, social sensing nominations select on demographic dimensions while one-hop selections are fully accounted for by network position. Social sensing thus buys higher centrality at the price of selecting on demographic dimensions beyond network position.

title: Artificial Intelligence as Monism: Ontological, Organisational, and Methodological Implications
affiliations: Université Paris I Panthéon-Sorbonne

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence as Monism: Ontological, Organisational, and Methodological Implications
detail.abstract: This paper argues that Artificial Intelligence should be understood as a form of monism: a unified substance that cannot be decomposed into separate elements such as data, algorithms, or technical architectures. Drawing from philosophical traditions of monism, dualism, and holism, the paper contends that AI is not merely a collection of components but a single, indivisible essence reflecting the phenomena it replicates. Treating AI as monism has deep implications across multiple dimensions. Epistemologically, it positions AI as the central interpretive force across technological, organisational, and societal domains, while raising ethical and existential concerns regarding singularity, the homogenisation of innovation, and the concentration of decision-making power. At the organisational level, a monistic approach challenges traditional siloed structures, advocating instead for transversal, problem-centric teams whose mandate derives from the integrity of the problem rather than from departmental hierarchy. In project management, it implies a unified vision and an integrated evaluation of complexity in which no single stakeholder perspective dominates the assessment of outcomes. In data and information management, it calls for architectures that reflect the irreducible unity of the phenomena being modelled. Ultimately, this paper calls for a paradigm shift in how AI is conceptualised, governed, and integrated, suggesting that only by embracing AI as monism can organisations achieve genuine agility and avoid the structural inefficiencies inherent to reductionist approaches.

title: Can Digital Innovations be a Gamechanger for Enhanced Openness, Accountability and Responsiveness of International Development?
affiliations: Georgetown University- Edmund A. Walsh School of Foreign Services and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Can Digital Innovations be a Gamechanger for Enhanced Openness, Accountability and Responsiveness of International Development?
detail.abstract: Enhancing collaborative methods that empower citizens to directly participate in decision-making processes of governments and international donor agencies is imperative to achieving better and more sustainable development results. Free and open access to data enabled through digital innovations has the potential to enable citizens to better hold governments and international donors accountable. Digital innovations such as interactive mapping and crowdsourcing provide unprecedented opportunities to democratize development. At the same time, digital innovations are associated with significant risk in terms of citizen’s privacy, data protection, and cybersecurity threats. This chapter presents a theoretical model for the emerging open development approach and discusses to what extent such a new approach represents a paradigm shift for international development. This chapter analyzes several case studies of digital innovations programs, such as Mapping for Results, Open Aid Partnership, and digitally enabled citizen-feedback programs, to investigate the on-the-ground impact of the paradigm. Finally, this chapter concludes with some early lessons learned and the challenges and obstacles these open development programs face in practice.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Accounting: Review of Implementation Challenges, Professional Risks, and Coping Strategies
affiliations: Islamic Azad University

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence in Accounting: Review of Implementation Challenges, Professional Risks, and Coping Strategies
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming accounting by automating routine work, improving financial reporting accuracy, strengthening fraud detection, supporting real-time analytics, and enabling more strategic forms of decision-making. Yet, the adoption of AI in accounting is not simply a technical upgrade. It represents a multidimensional organizational change that affects accounting systems, professional judgment, internal control, cybersecurity, ethical responsibility, legal accountability, employee competence, and the future identity of accountants. This narrative review synthesizes recent literature on the challenges AI may pose in accounting, drawing on empirical studies, conceptual papers, systematic reviews, and book chapters focused on AI, robotic process automation, generative AI, technology acceptance, managerial accounting, and accounting information systems. The reviewed literature indicates that AI adoption in accounting is constrained by several recurring challenges: data quality and data security risks, algorithmic bias, lack of transparency and explainability, high implementation and maintenance costs, integration difficulties with legacy accounting systems, workforce reskilling needs, employee resistance and morale concerns, overreliance on automated outputs, unclear liability, regulatory uncertainty, and the need for stronger internal controls. Although these challenges are substantial, the literature also shows that they can be mitigated through deliberate change-management strategies. Building on the Technology-Organization-Environment framework, the Technology Acceptance Model, human-AI collaboration perspectives, and internal-control logic, this review proposes an Accounting AI Change and Coping Strategy Framework. The framework suggests that responsible AI adoption in accounting requires six interdependent practices: readiness diagnosis, participatory system design, data and cybersecurity governance, explainability and human oversight, workforce reskilling and role redesign, and continuous monitoring. The review concludes that AI should not be framed as a replacement for accountants but as a socio-technical system that must be governed, explained, audited, and integrated into professional judgment.

title: The Concept of Information Poverty and How to Measure it in the Latin American Context
affiliations: Universidad Católica Boliviana and Georgetown University- Edmund A. Walsh School of Foreign Services

detail.title: The Concept of Information Poverty and How to Measure it in the Latin American Context
detail.abstract: The construction of the information society must be complemented with propoor vision and policies. For this reason, this paper defines the concept of information and communication poverty, introduces the criteria of poverty line location for its identification, and suggests computation for the economic cost of reaching such a line for its aggregate measurement. detail.abstract: The growing use of remanufactured-parts in collision insurance creates new opportunities for insurers to reduce repair costs and improve environmental performance; however, consumers' acceptance of remanufactured parts is heterogeneous and implicit claim contracts may cause insurers reputational losses. Designing a mechanism that balances economic profit, reputational risk, and sustainability becomes an important question. We develop a game-theoretic model with a manufacturer, a remanufacturer, and an insurance company, examining how insurers choose opaque remanufacturing (OR), where remanufactured-parts are used without explicit disclosure, or a transparent option (TO), where consumers choose new-part or discounted remanufactured-part insurance. Our results show that a higher claim probability paradoxically reduces insurance demand and insurer profit under OR through price escalation and reputational penalties, while under TO, it may shift demand toward remanufactured-part insurance when cost savings are high. Transparency is not always optimal: OR is more profitable when reputational penalty cost or discovery probability is low, whereas TO becomes more attractive when environmentally conscious consumers are more prevalent or remanufacturing brings greater cost savings. Claim probability affects model choice non-monotonically: OR is preferred at its moderate levels, while TO is preferred at its low or high levels. Although profitability and environment are not always aligned, TO is more likely to generate a win-win outcome when claim probability or environmental consciousness is high. These findings suggest that remanufacturers should enhance the cost advantage and reliability of remanufactured-parts, while insurers and policymakers should promote sustainable claim settlement through adaptive contract disclosure, insurance price discounts, and improved environmental awareness.

detail.abstract:
As artificial intelligence becomes the defining technology of our time, it risks replicating and accelerating the inequalities of the digital divide. This article advances a human-centred framework for understanding and addressing AI poverty-not as lack of access to AI infrastructure and tools, but as deprivation of key enabling factors necessary for meaningful AI use: i) strengthened informational capabilities, ii) pro-poor AI policies, iii) locally relevant data, iv) sustained capacity-building support, v) community-led AI adoption, and vi) strong protections for data privacy and civic digital rights.
Drawing on the capability approach and lessons from digital poverty research, the paper demonstrates that the emerging AI Divide threatens to deepen existing global inequalities. The expected benefits of AI are unevenly distributed; marginalized communities require far more than having access to AI tools to participate equally in the emerging AI-driven economies and to derive meaningful economic and social benefit from AI-enabled services. 
The article makes the case for shifting AI policy from a tool-centric to a people-centric paradigm. This requires five concrete priority actions: strengthening human AI capabilities and digital literacy; ensuring equitable access to information and locally relevant data; establishing regulatory frameworks protecting data privacy, civic digital rights, and human rights of local communities; fostering pro-poor institutional governance; and strengthening communities' capacities to adopt and appropriate AI solutions aligned with their needs and local socio-economic and cultural contexts. 
With policy evidence and actionable recommendations, the paper calls for a paradigm shift of AI policies —away from a tool-centric to a people-centric approach. Such a humancentered approach moving beyond “AI access” is essential for ensuring that AI’s disruptive potential does not widen existing inequalities. Deliberately shaped by policymakers and communities, AI can become a catalyst for poverty reduction and social inclusion—but only if we invest in people, not just platforms, and protect their fundamental rights.

detail.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI)-driven Decision Support Systems (DSS) have become essential tools in modern gas production management due to increasing operational complexity, real-time data availability, and the need for optimized decision-making. These systems integrate machine learning, predictive analytics, and optimization algorithms to enhance production efficiency, reduce downtime, and improve safety performance. This study presents a comparative analysis of AI-driven DSS approaches used in gas production environments, focusing on their performance, adaptability, accuracy, scalability, and integration capabilities. The research evaluates traditional rule-based DSS against modern AI-based systems such as machine learning models, deep learning frameworks, and hybrid intelligent systems. detail.abstract: Gas reservoir characterization and optimization are critical processes in the upstream oil and gas industry, directly influencing exploration success, production efficiency, and economic profitability. Traditional reservoir analysis methods often rely on simplified geological models and manual interpretation of seismic and well-log data, which may lead to uncertainty and suboptimal decision-making. In recent years, deep learning has emerged as a transformative technology capable of enhancing reservoir understanding by extracting complex nonlinear patterns from large and heterogeneous datasets. This study examines the role of deep learning techniques in gas reservoir characterization and optimization, focusing on their application in seismic interpretation, facies classification, reservoir property prediction, and production forecasting. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs), recurrent neural networks (RNNs), and hybrid architectures are identified as key models that significantly improve accuracy and computational efficiency in reservoir analysis. The findings indicate that deep learning-based systems outperform conventional approaches in terms of prediction accuracy, automation, and real-time decision support. However, challenges such as data scarcity, model interpretability, computational cost, and integration with legacy reservoir simulation tools remain significant limitations. The study concludes that deep learning plays a vital role in advancing intelligent reservoir management and highlights future opportunities in explainable AI, digital twins, and physics-informed neural networks for enhanced reservoir optimization.

detail.abstract: Sales forecasting accuracy is a critical operational challenge in e-commerce, particularly in high-velocity categories such as beauty products. This study evaluates the performance of the Holt-Winters Triple Exponential Smoothing method for sales forecasting in a Brazilian beauty e-commerce operation, comparing it against the company's internal forecasting methodology. Using 72 months of historical sales data (January 2018-December 2023) from "Beauty Brasil Online," a large-scale Brazilian online beauty retailer, we applied a structured forecasting framework across five product groups, seven categories, and eighteen subcategories, organized into three macro-groups to balance granularity and computational tractability. The study's test period covered the full 2024 fiscal year, encompassing more than R$5.4 billion in actual revenue and approximately 58.5 million units sold. Results demonstrate that the Holt-Winters additive model with optimized smoothing parameters (α = 0.45, β = 0.20, γ = 0.40) achieved a Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) of 0.6%, compared to 5.1% for the company's existing forecasting approach-an 88.2% reduction in forecast error at aggregate level. Accuracy gains were consistent across 10 of 12 months of the out-of-sample test period. Beyond model performance, the study proposes a managerial framework linking forecast precision to inventory optimization, revenue management, pricing strategy, and Sales & Operations Planning (S&OP) integration. These findings support the adoption of structured quantitative forecasting methods in e-commerce operations and contribute practical insights for marketplace strategy and retail demand planning.

detail.abstract:
This paper evaluates the structural implications of the revised taxation framework on the Indian cigarette industry, with particular focus on pricing economics, consumer adjustment, segment evolution, trade dynamics, illicit expansion, and medium-term profitability. The analysis examines how the effective linkage of GST to Maximum Retail Price (MRP), combined with elevated specific duties, alters realization efficiency, pricing power, and value distribution across the legal industry ecosystem.

Under the revised framework, effective tax incidence increases materially relative to the earlier regime, reducing the ability of manufacturers to retain value from incremental price increases and weakening pricing as a primary lever for earnings recovery. The study argues that the principal impact of the tax reset is not immediate demand destruction but a reconfiguration of consumption across major price bands and product formats. Consumer adjustment is expected to occur through delayed premiumization, format substitution, and migration toward lower-ticket alternatives rather than through a collapse in category demand.

The paper develops a framework for understanding how pricing architecture, affordability anchors, and segment migration interact under a highly regulated market structure. Particular attention is given to the role of entry and mass-market formats as absorption layers during the adjustment phase, the pressure on premium segments arising from weaker realization efficiency, and the implications of pricing discontinuities within the industry's price ladder.

The analysis further examines the consequences for trade economics, channel behavior, and the expansion of illicit markets. Retailers and distributors are expected to operate with higher working-capital intensity and a greater emphasis on inventory productivity, while illicit trade remains a key external variable affecting legal volume recovery and industry profitability.

Under the base-case scenario, the paper estimates a Year 1 legal industry volume decline of approximately 6–8%, accompanied by EBITDA compression of 200–300 basis points. However, the medium-term outlook suggests a gradual transition from adjustment to recovery as portfolio alignment improves, consumer migration stabilizes, and category economics normalize. The findings highlight the increasing importance of portfolio architecture, execution capability, consumer migration management, and channel efficiency in sustaining profitability within a taxation-driven market reset.

detail.title: The Geography of Market Power: Firm Location, Spatial Rents, and Their Social Costs
detail.abstract: The location decisions of spatially competing firms are intertwined, trading off proximity to customers against the cost of intensified competition near rivals, while economies of density across multiple plants add a further complication. We study these economic forces with new data on garage ownership since the 1994 privatization of London’s bus market. Exploiting the time dimension together with the exclusive use of garages by single operators, we model locations as choosing firms, rather than the reverse, yielding a tractable estimator despite rich spatial spillovers. Simulations show the highlighted trade-off is economically meaningful: each nearby competitor cuts the private return to capacity expansion by at least 10%. An optimal reassignment of garages yields up to 24.3% in welfare gains, though building restrictions and garage exclusivity leave non-zero local monopoly rents. When also pricing the externalities of empty “dead-mile” travel between garage and route, concentration reduces less, as large operators are best placed to economize on dead miles across their network.

detail.abstract: Logistics performance measurement is shifting from perception-based country rankings toward operational indicators that capture connectivity, movement speed, and delay conditions. This study examines how the transition from the legacy Logistics Performance Index to the World Bank's Logistics Performance Indicators 2.0 changes logistics performance assessment and its economic and environmental interpretation in 19 Arab and European economies. The analysis uses a three-stage design. First, it examines the legacy LPI panel for 2007-2023 to provide a historical logistics-performance baseline. Second, it uses 2023-2024 LPI 2.0 indicators to benchmark operational performance through maritime, aviation and postal connectivity, import dwell time, port turnaround time, transshipment time, and postal delivery time. Third, it links these indicators to GDP per capita growth and CO 2 emissions through exploratory cross-sectional models. The results suggest that operational logistics indicators reveal performance differences that are partly hidden by perception-based aggregate scores. Connectivity is positively associated with economic performance, while longer dwell time and port turnaround are associated with weaker economic outcomes and higher emissions. The environmental results are conditional: stronger connectivity is associated with higher emissions where logistics growth remains energy-intensive, while smoother operations are associated with lower congestion-related emissions. The study contributes by positioning LPI 2.0 as an operational dashboard rather than a replacement ranking system and by showing how connectivity, time performance, and regional structure shape logistics and sustainability outcomes. The findings are interpreted as exploratory associations because LPI 2.0 currently provides limited time coverage.

detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence governance has produced an expanding body of frameworks, regulations, and voluntary standards. Yet the harms AI systems cause-environmental, cognitive, criminal, and democratic-continue to grow alongside this governance activity. This paper argues that existing explanations for governance failure, while valid, are incomplete. Structural factors-jurisdictional fragmentation, information asymmetry, regulatory capture, and the speed gap between technological development and legislative response-account for much of the failure. But they do not account for all of it. 
This paper proposes that the absence of genuine orientation toward collective wellbeing among powerful actors may be one of the most significant and least examined variables in AI governance failure. When action is taken without genuine public interest behind it, even well-designed frameworks become instruments of performance rather than protection. The paper begins from a foundational standard: in a well-governed AI ecosystem, human lives must not be negatively impacted by decisions taken by AI or decisions taken for AI-directly or indirectly. Measured against this standard, no current governance framework is sufficient. 
The paper develops its argument through four moves: first, documenting how the nature of AI has produced a structural fragmentation of harm across five distinct affected groups-and how this fragmentation, whether or not tactically exploited, creates a positional advantage for companies that governance has not addressed; second, showing how an evidentiary structure systematically places the burden of proof on those least equipped to bear it; third, reviewing existing frameworks The Fragmented Veil | Page 2 and their shared blind spot; and fourth, proposing governance mechanisms designed to make the full picture visible simultaneously and to hold the orientation of powerful actors accountable over time. The paper concludes that mechanisms are necessary but not sufficient. The variable that determines whether a mechanism protects the public or performs protection is the orientation of those implementing it toward genuine collective wellbeing.

title: Valid Uncertainty for Marketing Inference When the Only Data Are Synthetic

detail.title: Valid Uncertainty for Marketing Inference When the Only Data Are Synthetic
detail.abstract: Synthetic respondents generated by large language models are judged by fidelity, how closely their answers reproduce human benchmarks, but a confidence interval asserts coverage, and coverage does not follow from fidelity. The gap between them has a structure that can be measured on one side and only bounded on the other. A controlled experiment that varies only the generating model shows that the choice of generator moves an estimate about five times as far as sampling does and can reverse its sign, while regenerating the same model moves it almost not at all, because under independent generation a new seed is simply a new sample. The dominant source of uncertainty is therefore the one a conventional interval holds fixed, and the reassurance a researcher can cheaply obtain certifies the wrong thing. The distance between the synthetic distribution and the population cannot be learned from synthetic data at all, because the population is precisely what the researcher lacks. The modulus of undetected error prices that distance, measuring the largest movement of an estimand among distributions that pass the same fidelity checks as the synthetic data. Two results establish the modulus as the exact cost of honest coverage: a diagnostic battery protects an estimand if and only if it identifies the estimand, and no interval shorter than the modulus covers the population estimand over the distributions the checks admit. Computed blind on the replication data of three published marketing studies and then unblinded, the modulus bounds the realized error wherever its premise holds and fails only where the premise itself fails, while mean-level fidelity leaves almost untouched the exposure of the quantities on which decisions turn, heterogeneity chief among them.

detail.title: Machine Learning Techniques for Predictive Maintenance in Natural Gas Infrastructure
detail.abstract: The reliability and safety of natural gas infrastructure are critical to ensuring uninterrupted energy supply and minimizing operational risks across production, transportation, and distribution systems. Predictive maintenance, enhanced by Machine Learning (ML) techniques, has emerged as a transformative approach for improving asset management and reducing unexpected equipment failures in the natural gas industry. This study explores the application of machine learning models in predictive maintenance systems used for monitoring pipelines, compressors, valves, turbines, and other critical infrastructure components. The research examines how supervised and unsupervised learning algorithms are utilized to analyze large volumes of sensor data, historical maintenance records, and real-time operational parameters to identify early signs of equipment degradation and potential failure. Techniques such as regression models, decision trees, random forests, support vector machines, clustering methods, and neural networks are widely applied to predict anomalies and estimate remaining useful life (RUL) of assets. The findings indicate that machine learning significantly enhances maintenance decision-making by enabling condition-based maintenance strategies, reducing unplanned downtime, and improving operational efficiency. Furthermore, the study highlights that predictive maintenance systems contribute to cost reduction, improved safety performance, and increased system reliability within natural gas infrastructure. However, challenges such as data quality issues, sensor reliability, integration with legacy systems, and cybersecurity risks remain key barriers to full-scale implementation. The paper concludes that machine learning-driven predictive maintenance represents a vital advancement in the digital transformation of the natural gas sector, offering substantial benefits in operational optimization, risk mitigation, and asset lifecycle management.

detail.abstract:
The gas industry is experiencing a significant transformation driven by the rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies. AI applications are increasingly being adopted across various stages of gas industry operations, including exploration, production, transportation, storage, distribution, maintenance, and safety management. This systematic review examines the current state of AI implementation in the gas sector by analyzing recent academic and industrial studies. The review explores the adoption of machine learning, deep learning, predictive analytics, computer vision, expert systems, and intelligent automation technologies that enhance operational efficiency, reduce costs, improve safety, and support data-driven decision-making. 

The findings reveal that AI has become a critical tool for predictive maintenance, equipment monitoring, leak detection, reservoir characterization, demand forecasting, and risk assessment. Furthermore, AI-powered solutions contribute to optimizing resource utilization, minimizing operational downtime, and improving environmental sustainability through better emissions monitoring and energy management. Despite these benefits, challenges such as data quality issues, cybersecurity concerns, integration complexity, high implementation costs, and workforce adaptation continue to affect large-scale deployment. 

This review highlights emerging trends, identifies research gaps, and provides insights into future opportunities for AI-driven innovation within the gas industry. The study concludes that the strategic integration of AI technologies can significantly enhance operational performance, safety, and sustainability, positioning the gas sector for a more intelligent and digitally connected future.
