detail.abstract:
The oil and gas sector is undergoing a significant transformation driven by rapid advancements in digital technologies, data analytics, Artificial Intelligence (AI), and intelligent automation. As the industry faces increasing pressure to improve operational efficiency, reduce costs, enhance safety, and meet sustainability objectives, organizations are increasingly adopting digital transformation strategies to modernize their operations. This study examines the role of digital transformation and intelligent automation in reshaping the oil and gas industry, focusing on the integration of advanced technologies such as Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT), cloud computing, robotics, digital twins, big data analytics, and autonomous systems. 

The study explores how these technologies are being applied across various stages of the oil and gas value chain, including exploration, drilling, production, transportation, refining, maintenance, and supply chain management. Digital transformation enables organizations to collect, process, and analyze vast amounts of operational data in real time, leading to improved decision-making, predictive maintenance, asset optimization, and enhanced operational visibility. Intelligent automation further enhances efficiency by reducing manual intervention, streamlining workflows, minimizing human error, and supporting autonomous operations in complex industrial environments. 

The findings indicate that digital transformation and intelligent automation contribute significantly to increased productivity, cost reduction, improved safety performance, enhanced environmental monitoring, and greater operational resilience. However, challenges such as cybersecurity threats, data management complexities, workforce adaptation, high implementation costs, and integration with legacy systems remain significant barriers to successful adoption. The study also highlights emerging trends, including AI-driven decision support systems, digital twin technology, edge computing, autonomous operations, and sustainable digital solutions that are expected to shape the future of the industry. 

The paper concludes that digital transformation and intelligent automation are becoming essential drivers of competitiveness and innovation in the oil and gas sector. Organizations that effectively leverage these technologies will be better positioned to improve operational performance, achieve sustainability goals, and adapt to the evolving demands of the global energy landscape.

title: From Microeconomics to AI Research: A Guide for Economists

detail.title: From Microeconomics to AI Research: A Guide for Economists
detail.abstract: The decisions that shape how modern AI systems are built and aligned are, in large part, microeconomic problems. These choices are being made now, at scale, and often without the formal tools economics has built for exactly this class of problem. This guide argues that economics has a distinctive and underused contribution to make to AI research, particularly in LLM post-training, alignment, and the economics of compute, and it shows economists how to make that contribution, whether from within economics, through collaboration with AI researchers, or in roles at AI labs. We begin with a self-contained primer on the RLHF pipeline, showing that its core components, reward modeling, preference aggregation, and policy optimization, rest on equivalences with discrete choice, social choice, and principal-agent models familiar to economists. Building on this foundation, we map specific microeconomic competencies to concrete AI research problems: behavioral economics for annotator biases, mechanism design for feedback elicitation, social choice theory for preference aggregation, contract theory and information design for AI alignment, game theory for multi-agent safety, and production economics for understanding compute scaling laws. For those who want to engage directly, we close with the practical foundations: the roles available in academia and industry, the technical skills they require, and a structured path for acquiring them, alongside a companion repository of programs and resources that we keep current.

declarations.funderStatement: This is an outcome of a major project UGC STRIDE C-1 at Tezpur University funded by University Grants Commission. The title of the project was "Reviving cultural artefact Gamosa through Intellectual Property management in Assam and innovative supply chain".

detail.abstract: Gamosa is an ethno-consumerism product of the handloom innovation system of Xipinie institution of Assam. Its cult status, identity, customs and weave finesse is lost to imitation Ghuni. Differentiation strategy of Gamosa is ineffective due to information asymmetry in its supply chain, tunnel vision policy with a weak Geographical Indications law and misappropriation of traditional cultural expressions in its neighbouring economies. The cheap cost of imitation Ghuni is due to synthetic yarn composition, mechanised production, and longer retail shelf life. We propose a trust-based participatory system to achieve information symmetry, traceability of yarn, weave pattern and origin of the designs for an evidence-based advocacy strategy. The NFT QR code design will give customer empowered purchase decisions with self-nudge retail behaviour. For domestic weavers and customary institutions, it opens heritage value e-commerce market. This frugal innovation will provide the rule of law to differentiate counterfeit Ghuni from Gamosa artefacts.

detail.title: Investment Targets as Reference Points

publicationDetails.detailsText: Fisher College of Business Working Paper No. 2026-03-013
publicationDetails.journalName: Ohio State University, Fisher College of Business Research Paper Series

publicationDetails.detailsText: Charles A. Dice Center Working Paper No. 2026-13

detail.abstract: We provide the first evidence of forward-looking reference points in investor behavior. Combining administrative data on option traders with a stacked difference-in-differences design, we show that investors' propensity to sell options spikes precisely when the underlying asset crosses the strike price, which retail investors frequently select to match their target price. The effect is difficult to explain using the standard disposition effect, nominal returns, salience, option Greeks, or complex option trading strategies. Moreover, the effect is present only for options bought out of the money, for which the strike price acts as a natural target, but absent for options bought in the money, for which it does not. The evidence is most consistent with investors evaluating gains and losses relative to a forward-looking target, in sharp contrast with the backward-looking purchase price widely used in the disposition effect literature. Our findings suggest that standard tests of reference dependence in selling decisions are misspecified when investors evaluate outcomes relative to reference points other than the purchase price.

detail.title: A Theory of Financial Deterrence

publicationDetails.journalName: MIT Center for Real Estate Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: I develop a theory of financial deterrence: the use of financial policy instruments, such as loan guarantees, to achieve military deterrence through their effect on defenseindustrial investment. The model features a government, a continuum of banks, a representative defense firm, and a strategic adversary. I embed two global games in sequence. In the first, banks coordinate on financing the defense-industrial base; in the second, the adversary conditions its attack decision on a noisy signal of the resulting military capacity. The core result is that a government loan guarantee simultaneously resolves both coordination failures through a single off-equilibrium commitment. In the unique equilibrium, the guarantee induces sufficient lending and capacity that the adversary does not attack-and because war does not occur, the war-contingent fiscal cost of the guarantee is exactly zero. Deterrence is achieved not by spending but by changing expectations. I extend the model to an alliance setting and show that Nash provision of guarantees is inefficient: each government freerides on its allies' commitments, generating a formal analogue of the NATO burden-sharing problem. The framework unifies several instruments of strategic economic policydefense development banks, export-credit agencies, and industrial guarantees under statutes such as the CHIPS Act-as applications of a single mechanism.

title: Faster, Fairer, Cheaper: The AI Revolution in U.S. Consumer Lending and Why both Sides of the Loan are Winning
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Faster, Fairer, Cheaper: The AI Revolution in U.S. Consumer Lending and Why both Sides of the Loan are Winning
detail.abstract: Traditional credit scoring systems, anchored to the Fair Isaac Corporation (FICO) model, impose structural limitations that systematically exclude millions of creditworthy consumers. Reliance on narrow bureaureported tradelines produces binary, static snapshots of creditworthiness that disadvantage thin-file applicants, recent immigrants, and young adults among the tens of millions of credit-invisible Americans. This paper argues a dual-benefit thesis: that artificial intelligence (AI) techniques, when responsibly deployed in consumer lending, simultaneously improve outcomes for both borrowers and lenders. Borrowers gain access to lower annual percentage rates, expedited underwriting decisions, and expanded credit availability, while fintech lenders achieve superior default prediction accuracy, reduced operational costs, and enhanced fraud mitigation. We examine the principal AI methodologies driving this transformation, including gradient boosting ensembles (XGBoost, LightGBM), natural language processing for automated document analysis, and alternative data integration spanning rent payment histories, utility records, and behavioral signals. Despite demonstrated performance gains, deployment of machine learning in regulated lending environments surfaces a fundamental Accuracy-Explainability-Fairness Trilemma: optimizing along any single dimension risks degrading the others, creating compliance exposure under the Equal Credit Opportunity Act (ECOA) and CFPB adverse action notice requirements. To navigate this trilemma, we introduce the Dual-Benefit Evaluation Framework (DBEF), a weighted scoring instrument assessing AI lending systems across borrower-centric and lender-centric dimensions. Analysis of published benchmarks and industry disclosures is consistent with the dual-benefit thesis while surfacing persistent disparate impact concerns. Future directions include generative AI for synthetic data augmentation [68], federated learning for privacy-preserving model training, and agentic AI for autonomous credit underwriting.

title: Taller and Higher in Status: The Impact of Stature on Occupational Outcomes
affiliations: Galatasaray University - Department of Economics and Galatasaray University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Taller and Higher in Status: The Impact of Stature on Occupational Outcomes
detail.abstract: Height is a cumulative health indicator shaped by early-childhood health conditions and genetic influences. In this study, we use cross-sectional data from the Turkish Health Survey (THS) to document height-based occupational sorting in terms of occupational prestige and task-based groupings in a developing-country context that has experienced a positive secular trend in adult height across generations. Our results reveal that height plays a significant role in both dimensions of occupational outcomes, even after controlling for various physical, mental, and socioeconomic factors. In line with previous research, we find that occupational returns to height are greater for men and that their impact decreases over time, in parallel with the secular trend in height for prestige scores. Task-based estimations suggest that height is positively associated with cognitive occupations and negatively associated with routine occupations, particularly through sorting into cognitive interpersonal occupations for men and cognitive analytical occupations for women. The findings suggest that policies aimed at reducing early-life disparities reflected in adult height may help mitigate persistent inequalities in labor market outcomes.

title: Temporal Nihilism: The Ontological Decomposition of Time Preference and the Emergent Catallactic Order
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Temporal Nihilism: The Ontological Decomposition of Time Preference and the Emergent Catallactic Order
detail.abstract: The persistent and systematic suppression of interest rates by central banks across the developed world represents far more than a mere technical failure of monetary policy. It constitutes a form of temporal nihilism; the ontological decomposition of authentic time preference and the erosion of the existential structure through which human beings relate to scarcity, finitude, and the future. This article develops a sustained interdisciplinary analysis that integrates Martin Heidegger's phenomenology of temporality in Being and Time with the praxeological framework of the Austrian School of economics, particularly the contributions of Eugen von Böhm-Bawerk, Ludwig von Mises, and Friedrich A. Hayek. Natural positive interest rates, when allowed to emerge freely in the market, serve as the honest price signal of human finitude, voluntary saving, and care (Sorge). By contrast, artificial credit expansion and the forced lowering of rates below their natural level falsify these signals, generating widespread malinvestment, illusory booms followed by painful busts, and a collective slide into inauthentic modes of existence. Drawing on empirical patterns observed since the 1980s and especially after the 2008 Global Financial Crisis, the article demonstrates how decades of ultra-low and even negative real interest rates have produced serial asset bubbles, corporate zombies, widening inequality, and chronic financial instability (Chancellor, 2022; Laubach & Williams, 2003). Ontologically, this process denies the reality of scarcity and colonizes the future through unsustainable debt accumulation, weakening the resoluteness and authentic projection that Heidegger identifies as essential to Dasein. In opposition to this nihilistic interventionism, the article defends Hayek's concept of catallaxy; the spontaneous, emergent order of the market, as the only institutional arrangement capable of preserving genuine intertemporal coordination without coercion. Catallaxy respects dispersed knowledge, honors voluntary time preference, and allows complex social cooperation to arise naturally from the mutual adjustment of individual plans. Ultimately, the defense of the catallactic order transcends narrow economic considerations. It represents an ontological and ethical imperative: the restoration of authentic Being-in-time against the nihilistic tendencies of modern monetary centralization. By reclaiming the real price of time, societies can move toward responsible projection into the future, sustainable capital formation, and a mode of existence that accepts rather than denies human finitude. This article contributes to the growing interdisciplinary dialogue between phenomenology and heterodox economics, offering both a rigorous diagnosis of contemporary monetary pathologies and a philosophically grounded path toward renewal.

title: Does Land Certification Improve the Environment? Mechanisms and Heterogeneous Effects from Satellite Data in Ethiopia
affiliations: University of Turin and Dire Dawa University

detail.title: Does Land Certification Improve the Environment? Mechanisms and Heterogeneous Effects from Satellite Data in Ethiopia
detail.abstract: Formal land certification is widely promoted as a means of improving tenure security and, through it, environmental stewardship and agricultural productivity. Yet evidence remains limited on two fronts: whether certification's environmental gains, as measured directly through remote sensing rather than self-reported investment, operate through an identifiable behavioural channel, and whether such benefits are shared across climate-constrained areas, disability-affected households, and beneficiaries of PSNP. This study addresses these gaps by integrating household survey data with satellite-derived environmental indicators. We examine vegetation greenness (NDVI), vegetation density (EVI), and biomass productivity (NPP) using linear regression endogenous treatment-effect, IV-2SLS, and OLS. Certification significantly improves all three outcomes across all three estimators. To identify the underlying mechanism, we construct a fruit-tree adoption indicator and implement a formal mediation decomposition. Certification significantly increases fruit-tree adoption, which mediates a meaningful share of certification's total effect on each outcome, indicating that fruit tree cultivation is an important, though partial, channel linking certification to environmental gains. These average effects mask substantial heterogeneity: safety-net beneficiaries and disability-affected households see smaller gains, while effects turn negative in semi-arid, low-rainfall areas — consistent with land clearing rather than conservation where climate constraints limit the returns to investment. Together, these findings show that certification's environmental dividends operate partly through fruit-tree adoption but remain substantially direct and are conditional on both household circumstances and local climate conditions. Certification programs should therefore be paired with targeted assistance for vulnerable households and complemented with climate-adapted interventions in water-constrained areas.

title: Biodiversity risk and bank credit allocation Sustainability commitments and double materiality
affiliations: Stockholm University - Stockholm Business School, Lund University - Department of Economics; Knut Wicksell Centre for Financial Studies, Lund University - Department of Economics and Stockholm Business School, Stockholm University

detail.title: Biodiversity risk and bank credit allocation Sustainability commitments and double materiality
detail.abstract: This paper examines how sustainability commitments shape banks’ incorporation of biodiversity risks into credit allocation. Using global syndicated loan data matched with firm-level measures of biodiversity impact and dependency, we find that all lenders extend smaller loans to more biodiversity-dependent firms, consistent with dependency risk being treated as financially material. By contrast, only UNEP FI–committed lenders reduce credit to high-impact borrowers, and only after joining, ruling out pre-existing greener preferences. This pattern is consistent with a double materiality perspective, whereby committed lenders respond not only to borrowers’ dependence on nature but also to their adverse impacts on biodiversity. The response strengthens over time and extends from GHG-related to non-GHG biodiversity impacts. Biodiversity risks have limited influence on secondary-market loan sales, except for modest evidence that committed syndicates sell loans to borrowers with high GHG-related biodiversity impacts. Overall, commitments mainly affect credit allocation at origination.

title: Time-Varying Loan Puzzles
affiliations: Kenyon College and Citigroup, Inc.

detail.title: Time-Varying Loan Puzzles
detail.abstract: This paper documents two novel empirical facts regarding the transmission of monetary policy to bank credit. Utilizing a structural vector autoregression with time-varying parameters and stochastic volatility, we show that the classic "loan puzzle”—an anomalous expansion of commercial and industrial (C&I) loans following a contractionary monetary shock—is absent prior to 1980. Furthermore, we identify a new consumer loan puzzle: the response of consumer credit to a policy tightening undergoes a striking sign inversion in the early 1980s and becomes persistently positive by the 1990s. Time-varying estimates reveal that the emergence of both anomalies coincides with the Volcker disinflation. Concurrent structural shifts in the monetary policy regime, financial deregulation, and the banking industry landscape fundamentally altered the credit transmission mechanism, giving rise to these post-1980 empirical puzzles.

title: A Large-Scale Macro-Finance Affine Term Structure Model of Interest Rates
affiliations: The Bank of Korea and Korea University

detail.title: A Large-Scale Macro-Finance Affine Term Structure Model of Interest Rates
detail.abstract: We propose a high-dimensional macro-finance affine term structure model that embeds a large vector autoregression for the joint dynamics of the yield curve and macroeconomic variables under no-arbitrage restrictions. Unlike prior studies that rely on a small number of macroeconomic variables, our approach reduces the risk of omitted variable bias and captures richer interactions between the yield curve and the macroeconomy. To address the curse of dimensionality, we develop a Bayesian estimation strategy that extends Minnesota-type shrinkage, preserves the analytical tractability of the marginal likelihood, and enables efficient posterior simulation. We demonstrate that the high-dimensional framework offers two distinct advantages over low-dimensional alternatives. First, incorporating a broad set of macroeconomic variables can improve out-of-sample yield curve forecasts when combined with the spanning hypothesis. Second, the richer information set enables a wider range of scenario analyses relevant to economic decision-making. To this end, we develop a formal method for conducting such analyses and provide two empirical illustrations: a yield curve steepening and a joint surge in oil prices and financial uncertainty.

title: Critical resonance as a transdisciplinary method for analysing food insecurity, environmental injustice and territorial development in the Global South

detail.title: Critical resonance as a transdisciplinary method for analysing food insecurity, environmental injustice and territorial development in the Global South
detail.abstract: This article develops critical resonance as a transdisciplinary methodological approach for analysing food insecurity, environmental injustice and territorial development in the Global South. Rather than comparing quilombola Brazil and Mozambique as empirically equivalent cases, the article places them in analytical resonance as distinct territorial formations that illuminate how hunger is produced through land dispossession, environmental exposure, climate vulnerability, infrastructure deficits, mobility constraints and uneven institutional protection. The proposed approach responds to two recurrent limitations in environment-development research: the reduction of food insecurity to household deprivation and the flattening of heterogeneous Global South territories into a single narrative of poverty, crisis or vulnerability. Critical resonance is presented as a method of analytical juxtaposition that preserves historical specificity while identifying shared mechanisms through which unequal environmental and institutional arrangements shape food and livelihood vulnerability. In quilombola Brazil, the analysis foregrounds racialized territorial dispossession, environmental racism and incomplete access to infrastructure and public protection. In Mozambique, it highlights climate shocks, conflict, displacement, rural livelihood vulnerability, market fragility and uneven district-level response capacity. The article proposes the concept of territorial food-health injustice to describe how food insecurity emerges where environmental risk, development inequality and institutional neglect converge. Its main contribution is methodological and conceptual: it offers a place-sensitive and justice-oriented framework for linking food insecurity to environmental development, sustainable territorial planning and policy responses in the Global South.
